results.summary_before: ChipTune is an 8-bit programmable sound generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It features two rectangular pulse generators, a triangle wave generator, and a noise generator, each controlled by four 8-bit registers. Configuration data is received via a UART interface at 9600 baud, and the audio output is pulse-width modulated. The design requires an external analog PWM filter and audio driver for testing, and it can be interfaced with a computer COM port.

results.summary_before: This design is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square-wave tone channels, a noise generator with white and periodic modes, and 16 levels of attenuation per channel. It is controlled via an 8-bit data bus with a write-enable pin, and it provides digital 8-bit audio output plus PWM outputs for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to produce sound, and the design includes a configurable clock divider. The project emphasizes hardware preservation and includes a comprehensive test suite, fitting on a single tile.

results.summary_before: This is a Tiny Tapeout Tensor Processing Unit that multiplies two 2x2 matrices of signed 8-bit elements to produce signed 16-bit results using a systolic array of four multiply-accumulate processing elements. It is controlled through an external microcontroller that sends input matrices sequentially in row-major order and receives outputs in the same order, with control signals LOAD_EN, TRANSPOSE, and ACTIVATION, and a DONE output. The design includes memory registers for the input matrices, a control unit, and a feeder module to schedule data flow. It achieves over 99.8 million operations per second when streamed and requires an external clock and coordination via the chip interface.

results.summary_before: DemosceneTTSKY is a fully autonomous VGA visual synthesizer that generates 640x480 video and bytebeat audio entirely from logic gates, with no RAM, ROM, or CPU. It uses an LFSR to randomly change visual equations, shift amounts, and palettes every second, creating evolving fractal patterns. The audio is output on bidirectional pins during video blanking intervals. The design requires a 25 MHz clock and external hardware such as a VGA monitor and a resistor DAC for RGB, plus an optional audio amplifier, and is notable for its self-directing demoscene nature.
